::: {.hero}
# Open Research Workflow

A step-by-step guide to making your research reproducible, citable, and open — from day one of your project to final publication.

::: {.badge-row}
<span class="tool-badge">Quarto</span>
<span class="tool-badge">Positron</span>
<span class="tool-badge">GitHub</span>
<span class="tool-badge">Zenodo</span>
<span class="tool-badge">renv</span>
<span class="tool-badge">R</span>
:::
:::

## Why this guide?

Open and reproducible research is increasingly expected — not just encouraged — by journals, funding agencies, and the scientific community. But the practicalities of *how* to do it are rarely taught explicitly during a PhD.

This guide documents a complete workflow that takes you from setting up a new project on **Day 1** through to archiving your code and data permanently when a paper is **accepted**. It uses realistic placeholder data from a freshwater ecology study so you can follow along with a real example.

::: {.callout-note}
This guide focuses on a **two-file Quarto approach**: an `analysis.qmd` for all your R code, and an `index.qmd` for your clean manuscript. This keeps your analysis fully transparent while your manuscript stays readable. It is designed for use in **Positron**, the modern successor to RStudio.
:::

## The tools

| Tool | Purpose | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| **Quarto** | Write manuscript and analysis together | Free |
| **Positron** | IDE with built-in Git and Quarto support | Free |
| **Git** | Track every change locally | Free |
| **GitHub** | Host code publicly, give reviewers access | Free |
| **renv** | Record exact R package versions | Free |
| **Zenodo** | Permanent archive with a citable DOI | Free |

Skip the blank-page problem. This is a working Quarto project — folder structure, `analysis.qmd`, `index.qmd`, placeholder data — that renders out of the box. Every file marks exactly what to replace with `FILL IN` comments.

## Who is this for?

This guide is written for **PhD students and early-career researchers** in ecology and related fields who:

- Use R and Quarto for analysis and writing
- Want to make their research reproducible without a steep learning curve
- Are preparing to submit to journals that require data availability statements
- Want a citable DOI for their code and data

## About this guide

This guide was written by [Olivier V. Raven](https://scienceecosystem.org) as part of his PhD research on kōura (*Paranephrops planifrons*) ecology and habitat restoration in Aotearoa New Zealand. 

The guide itself follows the workflow it describes — it is written in Quarto, version controlled on GitHub, and archived on Zenodo.
